mainTopic: Seating of the סנהדרין and its students, praise of the Jewish people, and the court's warning to witnesses in capital cases
overview: This amud finishes the משנה about the three rows of תלמידי חכמים who sit before the סנהדרין and move up one row whenever a new judge is needed. The גמרא brings the source for the half-circle seating from the פסוק "שררך אגן הסהר" in שיר השירים, and reads each word as a hint about the סנהדרין. One of those words teaches that a judge may step out only if 23 judges remain. The end of the פסוק, "סוגה בשושנים", praises the Jewish people for not breaking even a fence of lilies. רב כהנא uses it to answer a heretic. ריש לקיש and רבי זירא add more פסוקים showing that even the empty ones and the sinners of Israel have good in them, and a story shows רבי זירא's rough neighbors doing תשובה. אביי then explains that when one student moves up, all the students shift: it is better to be a tail to lions than a head to foxes. A new משנה begins with the court's strong warning to witnesses in דיני נפשות. It teaches that one life is like a whole world, because all humanity came from אדם הראשון alone.

steps.title: Three rows of scholars sit in front of the judges
steps.stepSummary: The משנה describes three rows of תלמידי חכמים seated before the סנהדרין, each person in his own fixed place.
steps.simpleTranslation: Three rows of Torah scholars sit in front of the judges, and each one knows his own place.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues describing how the סנהדרין sat. In front of the judges sat three rows of students, and each knew exactly where he belonged.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These rows are a standing reserve of future judges. Each scholar has a fixed seat, so it is always clear who comes next when a judge is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Knows his place, meaning his set seat by rank

phrases.english: And three rows of Torah scholars
sit before them

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד מַכִּיר אֶת מְקוֹמוֹ
phrases.english: each and every one recognizes his place

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשָׁלֹשׁ שׁוּרוֹת שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים יוֹשְׁבִין לִפְנֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's description of how the סנהדרין was seated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three ranked rows of scholars sit before the סנהדרין, each person in a fixed place.

steps.title: How a new judge is added and everyone moves up
steps.stepSummary: When a new judge must be ordained, he comes from the first row. Then one person moves up from each row, and a new person from the crowd fills the third row.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they needed to ordain a judge, they took him from the first row. One person from the second row moved to the first, and one from the third row moved to the second. Then they picked someone from the crowd and seated him in the third row.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains what happens when the court needs another judge. The best scholar in the first row joins the court, and everyone shifts up one row to fill the gap.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One empty seat starts a chain of moves. Each row passes one person up to the row above it. The last empty seat, in the third row, goes to someone chosen from the general audience.

keyTerms.meaning: To ordain, to appoint someone as a judge

phrases.english: If they needed to ordain
phrases.notes: He means ordaining an extra judge to sit on the court.

phrases.english: they ordain from the first row

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד מִן הַשְּׁנִיָּה בָּא לוֹ לָרִאשׁוֹנָה
phrases.english: one from the second row comes to the first

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד מִן הַשְּׁלִישִׁית בָּא לוֹ לַשְּׁנִיָּה
phrases.english: one from the third row comes to the second

phrases.aramaic: בּוֹרְרִים לָהֶן עוֹד אֶחָד מִן הַקָּהָל
phrases.english: they choose for themselves another one from the crowd
and they seat him in the third row

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּצְרְכוּ לִסְמוֹךְ סוֹמְכִין מִן הָרִאשׁוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the rows from step 1 exist: they are used to fill the court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A new judge comes from the first row, each row moves up one, and a new person from the crowd fills the third row.

steps.title: The one who moves up takes the seat that fits his rank
steps.stepSummary: The scholar who moves up to the first row does not take the empty seat of the man who left. He sits in the place that fits his own level.
steps.simpleTranslation: He did not sit in the seat of the first scholar. He sat in the place suitable for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds one more detail about the move. The person moving up does not simply take over the empty seat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seat of the man who joined the court belonged to the top scholar in that row. The newcomer is the lowest-ranked person in his new row, so he takes the place that fits his own rank.

keyTerms.meaning: Fitting for him, suitable to his level

steps.whatToRemember: The seating of the rows always follows rank. Moving up a row does not mean taking over someone else's honored seat.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא הָיָה יוֹשֵׁב בִּמְקוֹמוֹ שֶׁל רִאשׁוֹן
phrases.english: And he would not sit in the place of the first one
phrases.notes: "The first one" is the scholar who just left the first row to join the court.

phrases.english: rather he sits in the place fitting for him

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא הָיָה יוֹשֵׁב בִּמְקוֹמוֹ שֶׁל רִאשׁוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limit to the moving-up process described in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The one who moves up sits according to his own rank, not in the empty seat.

steps.title: The גמרא asks for the source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking where the משנה's rule about the semicircle seating comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: From where are these matters derived?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and asks for the source of the seating arrangement. This question sets up the next step, where a פסוק is brought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not about the rows we just read. It goes back to the earlier part of the משנה, which said the סנהדרין sat in a half-circle.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה
From where are these things known? The standard request for a source

steps.confusionAlert: "These matters" does not mean the three rows. It means the half-circle seating mentioned earlier in the משנה.

phrases.english: Gemara
From where are these matters derived?
phrases.notes: This points back to the משנה's earlier line that the סנהדרין sat like half of a round threshing floor.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְנָא הָנֵי מִילֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא's analysis of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for the סנהדרין sitting in a semicircle.

steps.title: רבי אחא בר חנינא brings a פסוק from שיר השירים
steps.stepSummary: רבי אחא בר חנינא answers with the פסוק "שררך אגן הסהר אל יחסר המזג".
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אחא בר חנינא said: As the פסוק says, "Your navel is like a round goblet, let no mixed wine be lacking..."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אחא בר חנינא gives the source, which is a פסוק in שיר השירים. Here he only quotes it. The next steps explain how each word hints at the סנהדרין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is a love poem, but here it is read as a hint about the סנהדרין. The key word is "הסהר", which hints at the moon's curved shape.

phrases.english: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina says
As the verse states
"Your navel is like a round goblet
let no mixed wine be lacking, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַחָא בַּר חֲנִינָא דְּאָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is the פסוק "שררך אגן הסהר" in שיר השירים.

steps.title: Reading each word of the פסוק as a hint about the סנהדרין
steps.stepSummary: "שררך" means the סנהדרין, which sits at the world's center. "אגן" means it protects the world. "הסהר" means it is shaped like the moon.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Your navel" is the סנהדרין. Why is it called "your navel"? Because it sits in the navel of the world. "Goblet" means that it protects the entire world. "Round" means that it resembles the moon.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the פסוק one word at a time. The last word, "הסהר", is the actual source for the half-circle seating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three wordplays. "שררך", the navel, shows the סנהדרין sits at the center of the world. "אגן" sounds like מגינה, protects. "סהר" means moon, so the court sits curved like a crescent moon.

keyTerms.meaning: The navel, or center, of the world

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the real answer to step 4. The moon's curved shape is the hint for the half-circle seating of the סנהדרין.

phrases.english: "Your navel" — this is the Sanhedrin
Why is it called "your navel"?
Because it sits in the navel of the world
"Goblet" — that it protects
phrases.notes: A play on sounds: אגן sounds like מגינה, "protects."

phrases.english: over the entire world
"Round" — that it resembles the moon

steps.triggerLanguage: שׇׁרְרֵךְ זוֹ סַנְהֶדְרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the פסוק quoted in step 5 points to the סנהדרין and its shape.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "הסהר" teaches that the סנהדרין sits curved like the moon, which is a semicircle.

steps.title: A judge may leave only if 23 remain
steps.stepSummary: "אל יחסר המזג" teaches that a member of the סנהדרין may step out only if 23 judges remain, the size of a סנהדרי קטנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Let no mixed wine be lacking" means: if one of them needed to leave, they check. If 23 remain, the number of a סנהדרי קטנה, he may leave. If not, he may not leave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the last part of the פסוק and draws a practical rule from it. A judge may leave only if enough judges stay behind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Mixed wine must not run short, and in the same way the court must never drop below a certain size. The minimum is 23, the number of a סנהדרי קטנה. If leaving would bring the count below that, the judge must stay.
steps.whatToRemember: The פסוק teaches two things. "הסהר" gives the half-circle seating, and "אל יחסר המזג" teaches that at least 23 judges must always remain.

phrases.english: "Let no mixed wine be lacking"
that if one of them needed to leave
they check
if there are twenty-three
corresponding to a small Sanhedrin, he may leave
and if not, he may not leave

steps.triggerLanguage: אַל יֶחְסַר הַמָּזֶג שֶׁאִם הוּצְרַךְ אֶחָד מֵהֶם לָצֵאת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the same פסוק, now its second half, and draws a new practical rule from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A member of the סנהדרין may leave only if at least 23 judges remain.

steps.title: The סנהדרין is like a heap of wheat
steps.stepSummary: The next words of the פסוק, 'בטנך ערמת חטים', teach that everyone benefits from the סנהדרין's explanations, the way everyone benefits from a pile of wheat.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Your belly is like a heap of wheat': just as everyone benefits from a heap of wheat, so too everyone benefits from the reasons and explanations of the סנהדרין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps explaining the same פסוק from שיר השירים, word by word, as a picture of the סנהדרין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier words of the פסוק described where the סנהדרין sits and what shape it has. This phrase describes what it gives: its Torah explanations feed the whole people, like food that everyone eats.

phrases.english: "Your belly is like a heap of wheat":
phrases.notes: This is the next part of the same פסוק, שיר השירים 7:3.

phrases.aramaic: מָה עֲרֵימַת חִטִּים הַכֹּל נֶהֱנִין מִמֶּנָּה,
phrases.english: just as with a heap of wheat, everyone benefits from it,
so too with the Sanhedrin, everyone benefits from their explanations.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה עֲרֵימַת חִטִּים הַכֹּל נֶהֱנִין מִמֶּנָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the word-by-word reading of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Everyone benefits from the Torah explanations of the סנהדרין, like everyone benefits from wheat.

steps.title: Not breaking even a fence of lilies
steps.stepSummary: The phrase 'סוגה בשושנים' teaches that the Jewish people do not break through even a weak fence made of lilies.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Set about with lilies': they do not break through even a fence made of lilies.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the last words of the פסוק as praise of the Jewish people: even a very weak barrier is enough to stop them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A fence of lilies could be pushed over easily, so it only works if people respect it. The point is that the Jewish people keep even small, gentle limits, like the extra fences the חכמים set up around the Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: A fence or border around something
Breaches, holes broken through a fence

phrases.english: "Set about with lilies":
that even with something like a fence of lilies,
they will not break through it.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״סוּגָה בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes reading the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Jewish people respect even a weak fence and do not break through it.

steps.title: A heretic questions the rule about a נדה
steps.stepSummary: A heretic challenges רב כהנא: how can the Jews allow a husband to be alone with his wife when she is a נדה? Surely they will sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what a certain heretic said to רב כהנא: You say a נדה may be alone with a man (her husband). Is it possible to put fire into wood chips and they don't burn?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a story that shows the idea of the fence of lilies. A heretic attacks a halacha he thinks makes no sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heretic argues that putting a husband and his forbidden wife together is like putting fire in dry chips: sin will surely happen. He is challenging the trust the halacha places in Jewish couples.

keyTerms.meaning: A heretic, someone who rejects the Torah
A woman during her monthly period, forbidden to her husband
Dry wood chips or flax that catch fire easily

phrases.aramaic: וְהַיְינוּ דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: And this is what a certain heretic said to Rav Kahana:
You say that a menstruating woman is permitted
to be alone with a man.
phrases.notes: He means her own husband, who is forbidden to her during this time.

phrases.english: Is it possible to have fire in wood chips and they don't blaze?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַב כָּהֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a story that illustrates the fence of lilies from step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The halacha allowing a husband and wife to be alone while she is a נדה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Human desire is like fire in dry chips; you cannot expect people to hold back.

steps.title: רב כהנא answers with the fence of lilies
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא answers that the Torah itself testifies that the Jews do not break even a fence of lilies.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The Torah testified about us 'set about with lilies', that even a fence of lilies they will not break through.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא answers the heretic using the same פסוק the גמרא just explained.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heretic's argument was based on ordinary human nature. רב כהנא answers that the Jewish people are different: the Torah promises they keep even weak limits, so a couple will hold back even when alone.
steps.whatToRemember: The fence of lilies means the Jewish people keep even gentle, weak limits, which is why halacha can trust them.

phrases.english: He said to him: The Torah testified about us
"set about with lilies,"
that even with something like a fence of lilies,
they will not break through it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הַתּוֹרָה הֵעִידָה עָלֵינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the heretic's challenge from step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Appeal to the Torah's testimony about the special nature of the Jewish people.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: People cannot control themselves when alone with someone they desire.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Jewish people keep even weak limits, so they can be trusted.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: even the empty ones are full of מצוות
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש brings a different פסוק: even the 'empty' people of Israel are full of מצוות like a pomegranate is full of seeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש says: from here, 'Your temples are like a split pomegranate': even the empty ones among you are full of מצוות like a pomegranate.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש offers another פסוק that shows the goodness of the Jewish people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads the word 'רקתך' (your temples) as if it said 'ריקנין' (empty ones). The point goes further than before: not only do the Jews keep fences, even the people who seem empty are packed with מצוות.

keyTerms.meaning: Pomegranate, a fruit full of seeds
Empty people, those who seem to have no good deeds

phrases.english: Reish Lakish says: From here:
"Your temples are like a split pomegranate":
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 6:7. The word for temples, רקתך, is read as if it came from ריק, empty.

phrases.english: even the empty ones among you
are full of מצוות like a pomegranate.

steps.triggerLanguage: רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר: מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different פסוק for the praise of the Jewish people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even the emptiest Jews are full of מצוות.

steps.title: רבי זירא: even the traitors smell good
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא brings a פסוק about יצחק smelling יעקב's clothes, and reads 'בגדיו' (his clothes) as 'בוגדיו' (his traitors).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא says: from here, 'And he smelled the smell of his garments.' Don't read 'his garments' but 'his traitors.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא gives a third source, going even further: even the sinners of Israel have a good smell before ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By reading בגדיו as בוגדיו, he teaches that even those who betray the Torah still carry something precious. This sets up the story about רבי זירא himself in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't read it as...; a way of finding a second meaning in a word

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira says: From here:
"And he smelled the smell of his garments."
Do not read "his garments" but "his traitors."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר: מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third source, going further than ריש לקיש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even the sinners of Israel have a good smell, a hidden value.

steps.title: רבי זירא befriends rough neighbors
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא was friendly with some hooligans in his neighborhood so they would repent, and the חכמים did not like it.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were some hooligans in רבי זירא's neighborhood. He kept them close so that they would return in תשובה, and the חכמים were upset about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story about רבי זירא, setting up the ending in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא acted on his own teaching that even sinners have value. The other חכמים objected to his closeness with them. The next step shows how it turned out.

phrases.english: There were certain hooligans who were
in the neighborhood of Rabbi Zeira,
and he would bring them close
so that they would return in repentance,
and the Sages were upset.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ בִּרְיוֹנֵי דַּהֲווֹ בְּשִׁיבָבוּתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells a story that shows רבי זירא living by his teaching about sinners.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי זירא drew sinners close to bring them to תשובה, despite the חכמים' objection.

steps.title: After רבי זירא's death, the hooligans repent
steps.stepSummary: When רבי זירא died, the hooligans realized no one was left to pray for them, and they did תשובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי זירא died, they said: Until now the short man with singed legs prayed for mercy for us. Now who will pray for us? They thought about it in their hearts and did תשובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends, showing that רבי זירא's way worked: the hooligans repented.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים objected to his closeness with them, but the result proved him right. His kindness had touched them, and losing him moved them to change, showing that even 'traitors' have good inside.

keyTerms.meaning: He passed away, literally his soul rested
The short one with singed legs, a nickname for רבי זירא

steps.whatToRemember: The three sources build up: the Jews keep even weak fences, even the empty ones are full of מצוות, and even sinners have good in them, as רבי זירא's neighbors proved.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּרַבִּי זֵירָא, אָמְרִי:
phrases.english: When Rabbi Zeira died, they said:

phrases.aramaic: עַד הָאִידָּנָא הֲוָה חֲרִיכָא קַטִּין שָׁקֵיהּ
phrases.english: Until now there was the short one with singed legs
phrases.notes: This is their nickname for רבי זירא himself.

phrases.english: who would pray for mercy for us;
now who will pray for mercy for us?
They thought it over in their hearts and repented.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּרַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story begun in step 14.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי זירא was right: bringing sinners close led them to תשובה, showing that even sinners have good inside.

steps.title: When one student moves up, everyone shifts
steps.stepSummary: אביי learns from the משנה about the three rows that when one student is promoted, every student behind him moves up one seat.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said there are three rows of students. אביי says: we learn from this that when they move, they all move.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the line in the משנה about the three rows of students. אביי draws a practical rule from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a student from the first row joins the court, his seat does not just get filled by one person. The whole line shifts forward one place. The first student of the second row moves to the last seat of the first row, and so on down the rows.

keyTerms.meaning: Rows (of students sitting before the court)
Learn from it; we can conclude from this

phrases.english: Three rows, etc.
Abaye says:
Learn from it
that when they move, they all move.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ כִּי נָיְידִי, כּוּלְּהוּ נָיְידִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the אגדה about רבי זירא to the משנה's rule about the rows of students.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When one student is promoted, all the students behind him move up one place.

steps.title: The demoted student's complaint
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the student who moves from the head of the second row to the end of the first row could complain that he went from the head to the tail.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him say to them: Until now I sat at the head of a row, and now you seat me at the tail?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אביי's rule. It points out that one student seems to lose his honor because of the shift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first student of the second row was the most important person in his row. After the move he becomes the least important person in the first row. The question is why he should have to accept this, since it looks like a demotion.

keyTerms.meaning: At the head; at the front
At the tail; at the end

phrases.english: But let him say to them:
Until now I was sitting at the head,
now you seat me at the tail?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵימָא לְהוּ: עַד הָאִידָּנָא הֲוָה יָתֵיבְנָא בְּרֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the fairness of אביי's rule that everyone moves.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's rule that all the students shift forward
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The shift seems to lower the status of the student at the head of the second row. He could refuse to move.

steps.title: Better to be a tail to lions
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the court can tell the student it is better to be the last among great people than the first among lesser people.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי says: They can tell him this: Be a tail to lions, and do not be a head to foxes.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the complaint with a well-known saying. He shows that the move is really a promotion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even the last seat in the first row is higher than the first seat in the second row. Sitting among greater people is more honorable than leading lesser people. So the student has nothing to complain about.

keyTerms.meaning: A tail to lions (the lowest among great people)
A head to foxes (the highest among lesser people)

steps.whatToRemember: When a student is promoted, everyone shifts up one seat. Moving to the end of a higher row counts as an honor, because it is better to be a tail to lions than a head to foxes.

phrases.english: Abaye says:
For they say to him like this:
"Be a tail to the lions
and do not be a head to the foxes."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: דְּאָמְרִי לֵיהּ הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the complaint raised in step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing: the apparent demotion is really a promotion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Moving from the head of a row to its tail is a loss of honor.
steps.terutzMaskana: The last seat among greater scholars is more honorable than the first seat among lesser ones.

steps.title: How the court warns witnesses in capital cases
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה describes how the court frightens witnesses in דיני נפשות. It warns them not to testify from guesswork, rumor, or hearsay, and tells them they will be closely examined.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does the court frighten witnesses in capital cases? They bring them in and warn them: Maybe you are speaking from guesswork or rumor, or repeating what another witness said, or what a trustworthy person told you. Maybe you do not know that in the end we will check you with careful questioning.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It describes the warning the court gives witnesses before they testify in a case where someone could be put to death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court lists the kinds of testimony that are not acceptable: guessing, rumors, and second-hand reports, even from a reliable person. A witness must have seen the event himself. The court also reminds the witnesses that they will be questioned closely, so any lie will come out.

keyTerms.meaning: They intimidate; they frighten (to make the witnesses careful)
Inquiry and interrogation; careful questioning of witnesses

steps.confusionAlert: Even testimony from 'a trustworthy person' is not accepted. In a capital case the witness must have seen the event with his own eyes, no matter how reliable his source is.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
How do they intimidate the witnesses
regarding witnesses in capital cases?
They would bring them in
and intimidate them, saying:
Perhaps you will speak from guesswork or from rumor,
a witness from the mouth of a witness,
phrases.notes: Meaning you heard it from someone else who saw it, and did not see it yourself.

phrases.english: or from the mouth of a trustworthy person,
perhaps you do not know
that in the end we will examine you
with inquiry and interrogation.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיצַד מְאַיְּימִין אֶת הָעֵדִים עַל עֵידֵי נְפָשׁוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה opens a new topic: warning witnesses in capital cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before capital testimony, the court warns witnesses against testifying from guesswork, rumor, or hearsay, and reminds them they will be closely examined.

steps.title: Capital cases are not like money cases
steps.stepSummary: The court tells the witnesses that a false witness in a money case can pay back and be forgiven, but in a capital case he carries the blood of the victim and all his future descendants forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that capital cases are not like money cases. In money cases, a person pays money and is forgiven. In capital cases, the victim's blood and the blood of his descendants hang on the witness until the end of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues the court's warning. It explains why capital testimony is so much more serious than testimony about money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A money mistake can be fixed by giving the money back. A death cannot be undone, and the false witness is also blamed for all the children and generations the victim would have had. That loss lasts forever.
steps.whyThisMatters: This idea, that one life includes all the generations that would come from it, is the basis for the famous lines later in this משנה about the value of a single life.

phrases.english: You should know
that capital cases are not like monetary cases.
In monetary cases,
a person gives money and is forgiven.
In capital cases,
his blood and the blood of his descendants
hang on him until the end of the world.
phrases.notes: 'His blood' means the accused person's blood, and 'on him' means on the false witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֱווּ יוֹדְעִין, שֶׁלֹּא כְּדִינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת דִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the court's warning to the witnesses with the reason capital testimony is so serious.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A false witness in a capital case is responsible for the victim's blood and the blood of all his descendants forever. In a money case, paying back brings forgiveness.

steps.title: Proof from קין: 'your brother's bloods'
steps.stepSummary: The משנה proves the idea from קין. The פסוק says 'דמי אחיך' in the plural, showing that קין was blamed for הבל's blood and the blood of his descendants.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we found with קין, who killed his brother, as it says: 'Your brother's bloods cry out.' It does not say 'your brother's blood' but 'your brother's bloods,' meaning his blood and the blood of his descendants.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a פסוק to prove what it just said, that a killer is responsible for the victim's future descendants too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah could have used the singular word 'דם.' Instead it used the plural 'דמי.' The משנה reads the plural as including the bloods of all the people who would have come from הבל.

keyTerms.meaning: Cain, who killed his brother הבל

phrases.english: For so we have found with Cain
who killed his brother,
as it is said: "Your brother's bloods cry out."
It does not say "your brother's blood"
but rather "your brother's bloods":
his blood and the blood of his descendants.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁכֵּן מָצִינוּ בְּקַיִן שֶׁהָרַג אֶת אָחִיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for the claim in step 20.
steps.raayaObject: That a killer is responsible for the victim's descendants as well
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 4:10, the plural 'דמי אחיך' said to קין

steps.title: A second reading: blood splattered everywhere
steps.stepSummary: The משנה offers another explanation of the plural 'דמי': הבל's blood was splattered on the trees and stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: 'your brother's bloods' means that his blood was thrown onto the trees and onto the stones.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a different way to explain why the פסוק uses the plural word 'דמי.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the plural does not point to future descendants. It describes the scene: הבל's blood was not in one place but scattered in many spots, so the Torah says 'bloods.' This second reading does not prove the point about descendants; it simply offers another meaning of the word.
steps.whatToRemember: The court warns witnesses in capital cases very strongly. A false witness carries the blood of the victim and all his future descendants, as we learn from 'דמי אחיך' said to קין. The משנה also gives a second reading: the blood was splattered on trees and stones.

phrases.english: Another explanation:
"Your brother's bloods":
that his blood was thrown
onto the trees and onto the stones.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר: ״דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternative explanation of the same plural word used as proof in step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The plural 'דמי' can also mean that הבל's blood was splattered in many places, on trees and stones.

steps.title: One life is like a whole world
steps.stepSummary: Because אדם הראשון was created alone, killing one Jew counts as destroying a whole world, and saving one counts as saving a whole world.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is why אדם was created as one single person. It teaches you that whoever destroys one soul from ישראל is treated by the פסוק as if he destroyed a whole world. And whoever keeps one soul from ישראל alive is treated as if he kept a whole world alive.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה draws a lesson from the fact that all of humanity came from one single person, אדם הראשון. A whole world came from one person, so one person counts as a whole world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the idea from קין in Step 21: a killer is responsible for all the descendants who will never exist. Here the משנה makes it a general rule using אדם הראשון, the clearest example of one person who became a whole world. The משנה also adds the positive side: saving one life is worth just as much.

keyTerms.meaning: One who destroys a soul (kills a person)
The פסוק counts it for him / treats him as
One who sustains or saves (a life)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is one of the most famous lines in the משנה. In context it is part of a warning meant to make witnesses feel the full weight of a false testimony in דיני נפשות.

phrases.english: Therefore Adam was created alone,
to teach you that anyone who destroys
one soul from Israel,
the verse considers him
as if he destroyed an entire world.
And anyone who sustains one soul from Israel,
the verse considers him
as if he sustained an entire world.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְפִיכָךְ נִבְרָא אָדָם יְחִידִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the קין lesson about lost descendants into a general principle based on the creation of אדם הראשון.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Destroying one life counts as destroying a whole world, and saving one life counts as saving a whole world, because all humanity came from one person.

steps.title: Creation from one person brings peace and blocks heresy
steps.stepSummary: אדם was created alone so that no one can claim a greater ancestor, and so that heretics cannot claim there are many powers in heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also done for the sake of peace among people, so that no one can say to his friend, 'My father is greater than your father.' And it was done so that the heretics cannot say, 'There are many powers in heaven.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives two more reasons why אדם הראשון was created alone: to keep peace between people, and to stop false beliefs about many gods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since everyone comes from the same single ancestor, nobody can boast of better family roots. And since only one person was created, nobody can claim that different gods each made different people.

phrases.english: And because of peace among people,
so that a person will not say to his fellow:
"My father is greater than your father,"
and so that the heretics will not say:
"There are many authorities in Heaven."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִפְּנֵי שְׁלוֹם הַבְּרִיּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds further reasons why אדם הראשון was created alone.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Creation from one ancestor prevents family boasting and blocks the belief in many divine powers.

steps.title: One seal, yet every person is different
steps.stepSummary: Creation from one person shows God's greatness: a human seal makes identical coins, but God made all people from אדם הראשון's seal and no two are alike.
steps.simpleTranslation: It also shows the greatness of הקדוש ברוך הוא. When a person stamps many coins with one seal, they all come out the same. But the King of kings, הקדוש ברוך הוא, stamped every person with the seal of אדם הראשון, and not one of them is like another.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives another reason: creation from one person shows how great הקדוש ברוך הוא is. It uses a comparison to minting coins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A human mint uses one stamp, and every coin comes out identical. All people come from one 'stamp' (אדם הראשון), yet every single person is unique. That shows a power far beyond any human craftsman.

phrases.aramaic: וּלְהַגִּיד גְּדוּלָּתוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
phrases.english: And to tell the greatness of the Holy One, Blessed be He,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאָדָם טוֹבֵעַ כַּמָּה מַטְבְּעוֹת בְּחוֹתָם אֶחָד –
phrases.english: for a person stamps several coins with one seal,
and they are all alike, one to the other,

phrases.aramaic: וּמֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
phrases.english: but the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, Blessed be He,

phrases.aramaic: טָבַע כׇּל אָדָם בְּחוֹתָמוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן,
phrases.english: stamped every person with the seal of Adam the first man,
and not one of them is like another.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְהַגִּיד גְּדוּלָּתוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further reason for creating אדם alone: it displays God's greatness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All people came from one 'seal,' yet each is unique, which shows the greatness of הקדוש ברוך הוא.

steps.title: Each person must say the world was created for him
steps.stepSummary: Because of all this, every individual must say: the world was created for my sake.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore, each and every person must say: 'The world was created for me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה draws a final conclusion from the lessons about creation from one person: every individual is important enough that the whole world could exist for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since one single person was enough to be the reason for creating the world, every person must see himself that way. For the witnesses, this means one life, including the defendant's, is worth a whole world, so they must take their testimony very seriously.

keyTerms.meaning: Must say / is obligated to say

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's speech to witnesses builds one big idea: every single human life is a whole world. Killing one person through false testimony is like destroying a world, and every person must see the world as created for him.
steps.confusionAlert: 'The world was created for me' is not about being arrogant. In this context it means every person is so valuable, and his actions so serious, that the whole world is at stake.

phrases.aramaic: לְפִיכָךְ כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד חַיָּיב לוֹמַר:
phrases.english: Therefore each and every one is obligated to say:
"For my sake the world was created."

steps.triggerLanguage: לְפִיכָךְ כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד חַיָּיב לוֹמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the practical conclusion from the reasons given for creating אדם alone.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Every person must view himself as one for whom the whole world was created.

steps.title: The court begins another point to the witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The court opens a new part of its speech: 'And perhaps you will say...'
steps.simpleTranslation: And perhaps you will say:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The court is getting ready to answer a thought the witnesses might have, which comes at the start of the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After frightening the witnesses about the weight of a life, the court expects a reaction from them. This line opens that new point; the actual worry and the court's reply come next.

phrases.english: And perhaps you will say:
phrases.notes: The court is still talking to the witnesses here. The thought it expects them to have comes right after this.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשֶׁמָּא תֹּאמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the lessons about creation back to addressing the witnesses directly, opening a new point.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduces a possible objection the witnesses might raise, which the court will answer next.
